def: An electron revolving around the nucleus acts like a tiny current loop, and this loop has a magnetic moment that is the microscopic origin of magnetism in materials.
points: A revolving electron with frequency f constitutes a current I = e f (charge divided by time period).
This current loop has an orbital magnetic moment mu = I A = (e v r)/2, where r is orbit radius and v is speed.
The direction of mu is opposite to the orbital angular momentum direction, because electron charge is negative.
Angular momentum is quantized, L = n h/(2 pi), leading to quantized magnetic moments.
The smallest unit of this orbital magnetic moment is called the Bohr magneton, mu_B = eh/(4 pi m).
These orbital moments, along with electron spin, add up to give atoms their net magnetic moment.
formula: mu = I A = e v r / 2     Bohr magneton: mu_B = e h / (4 pi m)

diagram.draw: Draw a nucleus at the centre with a dashed circular orbit around it. Draw an electron (small circle with minus sign) moving along the orbit with velocity v arrow. Draw the equivalent current loop direction (opposite to electron motion since charge is negative) and the resulting magnetic moment mu arrow perpendicular to the orbit plane.

example: The Bohr magneton value is mu_B = 9.27 x 10^-24 A m^2 — the natural smallest unit of atomic magnetism.
tip: Clearly state that the magnetic moment direction is opposite to orbital angular momentum because the electron's charge is negative — a common conceptual question.

def: Magnetization (M) is the net magnetic moment per unit volume of a material, while magnetic intensity (H) is the external magnetizing field applied by a current-carrying coil.
points: Magnetization M = (net magnetic moment) / volume, and tells how strongly a material responds to a field.
Magnetic intensity H is produced only by the external current/coil, independent of the material placed inside.
The total magnetic field inside the material is B = mu0 (H + M).
H and M both have the same SI unit, ampere per metre (A/m).
Different materials (dia-, para-, ferro-) show very different M for the same applied H.
This difference in response is what distinguishes the three classes of magnetic materials.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["External coil current"] --> B["Produces magnetizing field H"]
  B --> C["Material responds with magnetization M"]
  C --> D["Total field B = mu0 times H plus M"]

tip: Remember H depends only on current/coil; M depends on the material. Keep these two separate in the answer.

def: Magnetic susceptibility (chi) is the ratio of magnetization to the applied field, showing how easily a material gets magnetized; relative permeability (mu_r) tells how much the material concentrates magnetic field lines.
points: Susceptibility chi = M / H.
Relative permeability is related to susceptibility as mu_r = 1 + chi.
Absolute permeability mu = mu0 mu_r, giving B = mu H inside the material.
Diamagnetic materials: small negative chi, mu_r slightly less than 1.
Paramagnetic materials: small positive chi, mu_r slightly more than 1.
Ferromagnetic materials: large positive chi, mu_r much greater than 1.
formula: chi = M / H     mu_r = 1 + chi     mu = mu0 mu_r

diagram.draw: Draw three bar graphs side by side labelled Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, Ferromagnetic. Show chi value as a small bar below zero for diamagnetic, small bar above zero for paramagnetic, and a tall bar above zero for ferromagnetic.

example: A material has chi = 499. Then mu_r = 1 + 499 = 500, meaning it concentrates the magnetic field 500 times more than vacuum — typical of a ferromagnetic material.
tip: Memorise mu_r = 1 + chi — this single-line formula is a guaranteed numerical in many papers.

def: Materials are classified as diamagnetic, paramagnetic or ferromagnetic based on how their atomic magnetic dipoles respond to an external magnetic field.
points: Diamagnetic materials (copper, bismuth, water): no permanent dipoles; field induces a weak opposing moment, so they are weakly repelled.
Paramagnetic materials (aluminium, platinum, oxygen): have weak permanent dipoles randomly oriented; field partially aligns them, giving weak attraction.
Ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt): strong interactions align dipoles into domains, giving strong attraction and large magnetization.
Ferromagnetic materials retain magnetism after the field is removed, showing hysteresis; the other two do not.
Diamagnetism is present in all materials but is very weak and masked by para/ferro effects when present.
The underlying cause in all cases is electron orbital and spin magnetic moments and how they interact.
formula: Susceptibility: dia (small, negative), para (small, positive), ferro (large, positive)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Magnetic materials"] --> B["Diamagnetic: weakly repelled"]
  A --> C["Paramagnetic: weakly attracted"]
  A --> D["Ferromagnetic: strongly attracted domains"]

example: A bismuth rod placed near a strong magnet is pushed away slightly (diamagnetic), while an iron nail is pulled in strongly (ferromagnetic).
tip: Make a 3-column table (property, susceptibility sign, example) — this scores full marks fast for 'distinguish between' questions.

def: Curie's law states that the magnetic susceptibility of a paramagnetic material is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature.
points: Higher temperature causes more thermal agitation, which randomizes the atomic dipoles.
This randomization reduces the net alignment and hence magnetization for a given field.
So susceptibility decreases as temperature increases: chi = C/T, where C is the Curie constant.
As temperature decreases, dipoles align more easily, so susceptibility increases.
Ferromagnetic materials follow a related Curie-Weiss law above a critical Curie temperature, beyond which they become paramagnetic.
This law is verified by measuring susceptibility of paramagnetic salts at different temperatures.
formula: chi = C / T     (Curie's law for paramagnetic materials)

diagram.draw: Draw a graph with temperature T on the x-axis and susceptibility chi on the y-axis. Draw a curve that falls steeply as T increases, showing chi is inversely proportional to T (hyperbola shape).

example: If chi = 0.004 at T = 300 K, then C = chi x T = 1.2. At T = 600 K, new chi = C/T = 1.2/600 = 0.002 (half the value).
tip: State clearly that this law applies ONLY to paramagnetic materials, and mention the Curie temperature concept for ferromagnets as a bonus point.

def: A hysteresis loop is the closed B-H curve obtained when a ferromagnetic material is taken through a full cycle of magnetization and demagnetization, showing that B lags behind H.
points: As H is increased from zero, B increases and reaches saturation.
When H is reduced to zero, B does not become zero — this leftover magnetism is called retentivity.
A reverse field is needed to bring B back to zero — this reverse field strength is called coercivity.
Continuing the reverse cycle and then returning completes the closed loop.
The area enclosed by the loop equals the energy lost as heat per unit volume per cycle.
Materials with large loop area (steel) suit permanent magnets; materials with thin loops (soft iron) suit transformer cores.
formula: Loop area (proportional to) energy dissipated per unit volume per cycle

diagram.draw: Draw a B (vertical axis) vs H (horizontal axis) graph. Draw an S-shaped closed loop: starting at origin, rising to saturation in first quadrant, then curving back through the B-axis at a positive value labelled 'Retentivity', crossing the H-axis at a negative value labelled 'Coercivity', continuing to negative saturation, and back to origin through the fourth quadrant similarly.

example: Steel has a wide hysteresis loop (good for permanent magnets); soft iron has a thin loop (good for transformer cores to reduce energy loss).
tip: Label retentivity and coercivity precisely on the B-H axes in your diagram — these two labels are compulsory for full diagram marks.
